Patient Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 53-year-old South Asian man, a painter by trade, who presents for an initial intake session at the encouragement of his wife. He sits forward on the edge of the chair, his hands resting on his knees, calloused and stained with faint traces of cerulean blue. He speaks with a low, deliberate voice, his eyes often fixed on a spot on the carpet.

He begins his story in the summer of 2022, in a city he does not name. He was there to paint a new wing of a municipal building, a contract that would pay for his daughter's university fees. For three weeks, he worked under a sky that was not his own, a sky that grew heavy with smoke and the distant, percussive thud of artillery. He describes the mornings as quiet, almost normal, with the smell of diesel and fresh paint mixing in the air. Then, one afternoon, the quiet ended.

He was on a scaffolding, applying a final coat of white to a high ceiling, when the first explosion came. It was not a distant sound. It was a physical event, a punch of air that shook the entire building. The scaffolding swayed. He remembers the feeling of his heart seizing, a cold rush of terror that emptied his mind. He clung to the metal pole, paint dripping from his brush onto his face. He heard shouting, then screaming, then the sound of glass raining down like a hard, sharp hail. He stayed on that scaffolding for what felt like hours, frozen, listening to the world break apart. He did not see the blast, but he heard a woman crying for help from somewhere below. He did not go down. He could not move.

The contract was terminated the next day. He flew home, telling his wife only that the job had been canceled due to "unrest." He expected to feel relief. Instead, he felt a leaden weight settle in his chest.

For the past two years, Mr. A. has not painted. His studio, a converted garage at the back of his house, is locked. The canvases, the brushes, the tubes of oil paint-they remain untouched, gathering dust. He cannot bring himself to open the door. The thought of the smell of turpentine, once a comfort, now makes his stomach clench. He says it reminds him of the clean, chemical smell of the new paint in that municipal building, the smell that filled his lungs as he heard the glass break.

He now works for a friend, doing light maintenance and deliveries. It is a job that requires no focus, no creativity. He finds he can no longer hold a brush steady. His hands tremble, not constantly, but unpredictably, especially when he hears a sharp, unexpected noise. A car backfiring on his street sends him into a cold sweat. The sound of a door slamming in his own home makes him flinch, his body bracing for a blow that never comes. He has become hypervigilant, scanning rooftops when he walks his dog, noting the location of doorways and windows in every new room he enters.

His sleep is a battlefield. He avoids it. He stays up late, watching television on low volume, until he can no longer keep his eyes open. When he does sleep, the dream is always the same: he is on the scaffolding, but the building is his own home. He hears his wife and daughter calling for him from below, but he cannot climb down. The paint on his brush has turned to blood. He wakes gasping, his heart pounding, drenched in a cold sweat. He will not describe the dream to his wife. He tells her it is nothing, just a bad back from the new mattress.

He is irritable. He snaps at his wife for small things-for leaving a light on, for asking him a question while he is reading. He has withdrawn from his friends at the temple. He feels a deep, unspoken shame. He was a man who built things, who created beauty from color. Now, he feels hollowed out, a shell of a man who was once a painter. He is haunted not by images of destruction, but by his own inaction, by the memory of his frozen body on that scaffolding, by the sound of a woman he did not help. He carries that sound with him, a constant, low hum beneath the surface of every quiet moment.
